questions.question: Which Danish king's nickname gave its name to Bluetooth wireless technology?
questions.explanation: The Bluetooth logo joins the old runes for H and B. Harald united the Danes about 1,000 years ago.

questions.question: Margrete I ruled which three countries at the same time?
questions.explanation: In 1397 the three kingdoms joined in the Kalmar Union. Margrete ruled them until she died in 1412.

questions.question: Which king built Rosenborg Castle in Copenhagen as a summer home?
questions.explanation: Christian IV was king for about 60 years. He built many castles, towers and new towns.

questions.question: Until 1944, Iceland was linked to which other country?
questions.explanation: On 17 June 1944 Iceland became a republic. Icelanders celebrate that day as their national day.

questions.question: In April 1940 soldiers from which country marched into Denmark?
questions.explanation: Denmark was occupied until May 1945. The Danish army stopped fighting after only a few hours.

questions.question: On the evening of 4 May, Danes put what in their windows to remember the end of the war in 1945?
questions.explanation: During the war people had to cover their windows at night. Candles in the window mean light and freedom.

questions.question: King Canute the Great ruled Denmark, Norway and which country across the North Sea?
questions.explanation: Canute became king of England in 1016. His three lands are called the North Sea Empire.

questions.question: Which big Swedish warship sank on its first voyage in 1628?
questions.explanation: The Vasa lay on the seabed for over 300 years. It was lifted in 1961 and placed in a museum in Stockholm.

questions.question: In 1917 Finland declared itself independent from which large country?
questions.explanation: Finland's Independence Day is 6 December. Before 1917 Finland had been part of the Russian Empire for over 100 years.

questions.question: Many Danish kings and queens are buried in a big cathedral in which city?
questions.explanation: Roskilde Cathedral has the tombs of many monarchs, including Margrete I and Christian IV.

questions.question: Shakespeare's play Hamlet is set at which Danish castle?
questions.explanation: Kronborg is in Helsingør, which English writers called Elsinore. Hamlet is a prince of Denmark in the play.

questions.question: Tycho Brahe, a Danish nobleman in the 1500s, spent his life studying what?
questions.explanation: He built an observatory on the island of Ven and measured the sky before the telescope was invented.

questions.question: What does the name Copenhagen mean in old Danish?
questions.explanation: Copenhagen began as a small fishing and trading town. Bishop Absalon built a castle there around 1167.

questions.question: Until 1658, Malmö and the land around it belonged to Denmark. What is this region called?
questions.explanation: Denmark lost it to Sweden after a war, in the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658.

questions.question: In 1969 oil was found under the North Sea off which Nordic country, making it rich?
questions.explanation: The Ekofisk field started a new oil industry in Norway. The country later saved some of the oil money for the future.

questions.question: Which famous amusement park opened in Copenhagen in 1843?
questions.explanation: Its founder Georg Carstensen wanted a place for fun and music in the middle of the city.

questions.question: Carl Linnaeus, a Swede in the 1700s, became famous for sorting and naming what?
questions.explanation: He gave plants and animals two-part Latin names, like Homo sapiens for humans. Scientists all over the world use this system.

questions.question: The Round Tower in Copenhagen has a wide ramp inside instead of stairs. What was it first built as?
questions.explanation: King Christian IV had it built in 1642, together with a church and a library.

questions.question: Harald Bluetooth had a big carved stone raised for his parents in which small Danish town?
questions.explanation: It is often called Denmark's birth certificate. It stands by a church, between two big burial mounds.

questions.question: Which Danish writer of fairy tales was born in Odense in 1805?
questions.explanation: He wrote The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling. His tales have been translated into over 100 languages.

questions.question: Which animal is shown three times on Denmark's national coat of arms?
questions.explanation: The three blue lions have been a Danish royal symbol for over 800 years.

questions.question: Which famous toy name comes from the Danish words 'leg godt', meaning 'play well'?
questions.explanation: Ole Kirk Christiansen, a carpenter in Billund, began making wooden toys in 1932. Plastic bricks came later.

questions.question: Sweden did not take sides in World War II. What do we call a country like that?
questions.explanation: Sweden also stayed out of World War I.

questions.question: In the winter of 1658 a Swedish army marched to the island of Zealand across what?
questions.explanation: The army crossed the ice of the Great Belt. It was a daring march, and the Danes were very surprised.

questions.question: Which Indigenous people have lived in northern Norway, Sweden and Finland for thousands of years?
questions.explanation: Many Sami have herded reindeer for hundreds of years. Their homeland is called Sápmi.

questions.question: In 1939 which big country attacked Finland in the Winter War?
questions.explanation: The Finns fought hard in deep snow. They kept their independence but gave up some land in 1940.

questions.question: Copenhagen's old stock exchange, Børsen, had a spire shaped like the twisted tails of which animals?
questions.explanation: Christian IV had Børsen built for merchants in the 1600s. On its spire, four dragons twisted their tails together to a point.

questions.question: The Danish money called 'krone' is named after what royal object?
questions.explanation: In the 1870s Denmark, Sweden and Norway formed a money union, and all three began to use the krone or krona.

questions.question: Trelleborg, a Danish fortress from about the year 980, was built in what shape?
questions.explanation: It had a round wall with four gates and long houses inside. It is thought that Harald Bluetooth had it built.

questions.question: Which animal holds an axe on Norway's coat of arms?
questions.explanation: The axe is the sign of King Olav II, later called Saint Olav. He died in a battle in 1030.

questions.question: The Danevirke was built to protect the south of Denmark. What was it?
questions.explanation: Parts of it are more than 1,200 years old. Harald Bluetooth later made it stronger.

questions.question: The Celsius temperature scale is named after a scientist from which Nordic country?
questions.explanation: Anders Celsius was an astronomer in Uppsala in the 1700s.

questions.question: In 1917 Denmark sold its islands in the Caribbean Sea to which country?
questions.explanation: The islands became the US Virgin Islands. The United States paid about 25 million dollars in gold.

questions.question: What destroyed a large part of Copenhagen in 1728?
questions.explanation: The fire burned for several days and many people lost their homes. The city was built up again.

questions.question: On 17 May, which country celebrates its national day with big children's parades?
questions.explanation: The day marks 17 May 1814, when Norway signed its own constitution. Children march through the towns with flags.

questions.question: In 1801 the British admiral Nelson fought a battle outside which Nordic capital?
questions.explanation: Legend says Nelson held his telescope to his blind eye so he could not see the order to stop. Britain won.

questions.question: Gorm the Old is often called the first king of Denmark. Which famous king was his son?
questions.explanation: Gorm died around the year 958. His son Harald then ruled Denmark for almost 30 years.

questions.question: The Althing was started in Iceland around the year 930. What was it?
questions.explanation: Chieftains and farmers met every summer at Þingvellir to make laws and settle arguments.

questions.question: In which Swedish town was the union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden agreed in 1397?
questions.explanation: The Kalmar Union lasted for over 100 years.

questions.question: After a big fire in 1624, King Christian IV built a new town where Oslo lies. What did he call it?
questions.explanation: Christiania got back the name Oslo in 1925.

questions.question: When Norway left its union with Sweden, it chose a prince from which country as its king?
questions.explanation: He took the name Haakon VII, after old Norwegian kings. His wife, Maud, was a British princess.

questions.question: In 1814 Denmark lost Norway but kept Iceland, Greenland and which North Atlantic islands?
questions.explanation: Norway went to the Swedish king, but Norwegians wrote their own constitution that year.

questions.question: Frederik VII signed Denmark's first constitution in 1849. What did it end?
questions.explanation: Only some men could vote at first. Women got the vote much later.

questions.question: In the war of 1864, Denmark lost Schleswig and Holstein to Prussia and which other country?
questions.explanation: Denmark lost the battle at Dybbøl in April 1864 and had to give up the lands in the south.

questions.question: In 1906 which country in Europe was first to give women the right to vote in national elections?
questions.explanation: In 1907 Finland also elected 19 women to parliament, the first in Europe.

questions.question: Ships sailing through the Øresund had to pay a toll to the Danish king. Which castle guarded the strait?
questions.explanation: The toll lasted from the 1400s until 1857 and made the Danish kings rich.

questions.question: Which Swedish king, known as a daring soldier, was killed in Norway in 1718?
questions.explanation: He spent most of his rule at war with Russia, Denmark and Poland.

questions.question: Which Swedish diplomat led the United Nations from 1953 until his death in a plane crash in 1961?
questions.explanation: He was given the Nobel Peace Prize after his death.

questions.question: In 1812 the Russian emperor made which city the capital of Finland?
questions.explanation: Finland had been ruled by Sweden until 1809. Turku was the main city before Helsinki, which lies closer to Saint Petersburg.

questions.question: In 1835 Elias Lönnrot published which Finnish national epic, made from old folk poems?
questions.explanation: The Kalevala made many Finns proud of their own language long before independence.

questions.question: Which two Nordic countries joined the EU in 1995, together with Austria?
questions.explanation: Norway also voted on joining in 1994, but the answer was no.

questions.question: In which year did Sweden change from driving on the left to driving on the right?
questions.explanation: Everyone stopped at 4.50 in the morning, changed sides and drove on at 5.00. Ordinary traffic was banned for a few hours that night.

questions.question: What did Iceland and Britain argue about in the Cod Wars from the 1950s to the 1970s?
questions.explanation: Iceland made its fishing limits bigger several times, because fish were its main export.

questions.question: Which country's soldiers came to the Faroe Islands in 1940 and stayed during World War II?
questions.explanation: Britain wanted to stop Germany from using the islands. The Faroes got home rule in 1948.

questions.question: In August 1943 Danish sailors did what to many of their navy's ships, so Germany could not use them?
questions.explanation: It happened on 29 August 1943, the day Germany declared a state of emergency in Denmark. A few ships escaped to Sweden.

questions.question: In October 1943 fishing boats carried thousands of Danish Jews to safety in which country?
questions.explanation: Many Danes helped to hide them and to pay the fishermen. Most of Denmark's Jews were saved.

questions.question: In 1973 Denmark joined the European Economic Community together with which two countries?
questions.explanation: Norway had planned to join as well, but its voters said no in 1972.

questions.question: Which three Nordic countries were among the twelve founders of NATO in 1949?
questions.explanation: Sweden and Finland stayed outside for many decades.

questions.question: In 1676 the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer showed that what has a speed?
questions.explanation: He saw that Jupiter's moon Io appeared late when Jupiter was far from Earth. Light needs time to travel.

questions.question: Harald Bluetooth's big rune stone says he made the Danes what?
questions.explanation: The three-sided stone is from the second half of the 900s. One side shows Christ, one of the oldest pictures of him in Scandinavia.

questions.question: In 1620 Denmark started a trading colony at Tranquebar in which country?
questions.explanation: Tranquebar was Danish for over 200 years. In 1845 Denmark sold it to Britain.

questions.question: How did Northern Schleswig return to Denmark in 1920?
questions.explanation: After World War I people voted in two zones. The north chose Denmark and the south chose Germany.

questions.question: Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg saved thousands of Jews in 1944 in which city?
questions.explanation: He handed out protective passports and rented safe houses. He disappeared in 1945.

questions.question: After Christiansborg Palace burned in 1794, the Danish royal family moved to which palace?
questions.explanation: Amalienborg was first built for four noble families in the 1750s. It has four matching palaces around a square.

questions.question: Which Danish king, nicknamed Forkbeard, was accepted as king of England in 1013?
questions.explanation: He died only a few weeks later.

questions.question: Gorm the Old raised a small rune stone at Jelling for his wife. What was her name?
questions.explanation: The stone calls her the adornment of Denmark. Their son Harald later raised the big stone.

questions.question: During the occupation of Denmark, which king rode through Copenhagen on his horse every morning?
questions.explanation: Many Danes saw this as a sign that the king stayed with his people.

questions.question: Which town on the west coast of Jutland is often called the oldest town in Denmark?
questions.explanation: Ribe was already a trading place around the year 700.

questions.question: Norway's constitution of 1814 was written in which village?
questions.explanation: It is among the oldest written constitutions in Europe.

questions.question: In which year did Norway end its union with Sweden?
questions.explanation: Norwegians voted on it, and almost everyone who voted said yes.

questions.question: Iceland's national day, 17 June, is the birthday of which independence hero?
questions.explanation: He was born in 1811 and led Iceland's fight for self-rule in the 1800s.

questions.question: In 1866 the Danish princess Dagmar married a crown prince. Later she became empress of which country?
questions.explanation: She took the name Maria Feodorovna. Her son Nicholas II was the last Russian tsar.

questions.question: In 1807 Britain attacked Copenhagen to take away what?
questions.explanation: Britain feared Napoleon would use the ships. After this Denmark sided with France, which later cost it Norway.

questions.question: In the 1600s Sweden was a great power that controlled lands around which sea?
questions.explanation: Besides Finland, Sweden ruled Estonia and parts of Latvia, Russia and northern Germany.

questions.question: In 1972 Margrethe II became queen of Denmark after the death of her father. What was his name?
questions.explanation: She was the first woman to rule Denmark since Margrete I.

questions.question: Before the euro, what was the money of Finland called?
questions.explanation: Finland got its own markka in 1860, while it was ruled by Russia. Euro notes and coins replaced it in 2002.

questions.question: Soviet soldiers stayed on which Danish island until 1946?
questions.explanation: They came in May 1945 to take over from the German army and left in April 1946.

questions.question: Johann Friedrich Struensee, a German doctor, ruled Denmark in 1770-72 in the name of which king?
questions.explanation: He brought in many reforms, including freedom of the press, before he was removed and executed in 1772.

questions.question: In 1788 Denmark ended the 'stavnsbånd'. It had tied which group to the land where they were born?
questions.explanation: The 1788 law freed them step by step, fully by 1800. It was one of the big farm reforms of the time.

questions.question: In 1792 Denmark-Norway decided to end which trade, from 1803?
questions.explanation: It was the first European country to decide this. Slavery itself continued in its colonies until 1848.

questions.question: N. F. S. Grundtvig, a Danish priest and poet of the 1800s, is known as the father of which type of school?
questions.explanation: The first folk high school opened in Rødding in 1844. Adults, mostly young farmers, studied there together.

questions.question: Which Danish king introduced the Lutheran Reformation in 1536?
questions.explanation: After a civil war he took over church property and made Denmark and Norway Lutheran.

questions.question: Which Swedish nobleman led the rebellion against Danish rule and was elected king in 1523?
questions.explanation: His election broke up the Kalmar Union. Sweden's national day, 6 June, marks the date.

questions.question: Which Swedish king died at the Battle of Lützen in Germany in 1632?
questions.explanation: Sweden won the battle, but its king, called the Lion of the North, was killed.

questions.question: Which Danish king became absolute ruler in 1660, after the war with Sweden?
questions.explanation: He won the support of townspeople and the clergy. The King's Law of 1665 made the new rule official.

questions.question: In 1943 Norwegian saboteurs attacked a plant at Vemork that made what?
questions.explanation: Heavy water was thought to be useful for atomic bomb research. In 1965 the story was made into the film The Heroes of Telemark.

questions.question: In 1980 Iceland elected Vigdís Finnbogadóttir. What made her election special?
questions.correct: First woman president chosen by voters
wrong: First Icelander to lead the UN
questions.explanation: She served four terms, from 1980 to 1996. In Iceland the president is chosen by a vote of the people.

questions.question: In 1783 a huge eruption in Iceland caused famine there and a strange haze over Europe. What is the eruption called?
questions.explanation: Many Icelanders died of hunger in the years after the eruption.

questions.question: In 1982 Greenlanders voted to leave which European organisation, which they did in 1985?
questions.explanation: Greenland had joined in 1973 with Denmark, even though most Greenlanders had voted no.

questions.question: Why did the Dano-Norwegian priest Hans Egede sail to Greenland in 1721?
questions.correct: To look for lost Norse Christians
wrong: To find a sea route to China
questions.explanation: He found no Norse people, only Inuit, so he started a Lutheran mission among them.

questions.question: In 1951 the USA began building a large air base in northwest Greenland. What was it called?
questions.explanation: It followed a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the USA, early in the Cold War.

questions.question: In 1921 the League of Nations decided that the Swedish-speaking Åland Islands should belong to which country?
questions.explanation: The islands were given wide self-rule and were to stay free of military forces.

questions.question: Founded in 1477, which university is the oldest in the Nordic countries?
questions.explanation: The University of Copenhagen followed only two years later, in 1479.

questions.question: Sweden's Riksbank, founded in 1668, is often called the oldest what?
questions.explanation: Sweden was also early with banknotes, issued from 1661.

questions.question: In the 1950s the Nordic countries agreed that their citizens could cross borders without what?
questions.explanation: The Nordic Council, where members of the Nordic parliaments meet, was set up in 1952.

questions.question: At the end of the Winter War in 1940, Finland gave up much of which region to the Soviet Union?
questions.explanation: Many people left their homes in Karelia and moved to other parts of Finland.

questions.question: In 1626 Christian IV's army lost the battle at Lutter. Which big European war was it part of?
questions.explanation: Denmark left the war with the Peace of Lübeck in 1629.

questions.question: In 1863 a Danish prince became king of Greece. Under which name did he rule?
questions.explanation: He was the son of Christian IX and ruled Greece for about 50 years.

questions.question: In which Swedish town did Norway and Sweden agree in 1905 on a peaceful end to their union?
questions.explanation: The Karlstad agreement avoided a war between the two countries.

questions.question: Who was elected king of Norway at Eidsvoll in 1814?
questions.explanation: He was king for only a few months. After a short war with Sweden he gave up the throne.

questions.question: In 1810 Sweden chose a French marshal as heir to the throne. What was his family name?
questions.explanation: He became king in 1818 as Charles XIV John. His family name became the name of Sweden's royal house.

questions.question: Which Danish admiral won the Battle of Køge Bay against Sweden in 1677?
questions.explanation: Juel's victory gave Denmark control of the sea in the Scanian War.

questions.question: The Danish tale of Amleth, which inspired Hamlet, was written down around 1200 by whom?
questions.explanation: Saxo worked for Bishop Absalon and wrote a long history of the Danes.

questions.question: After giving up her throne in 1654, Sweden's Queen Christina settled in which city?
questions.explanation: She had become Catholic and spent most of the rest of her life in Rome, supporting art and science.

questions.question: In 1361 King Valdemar IV took the rich trading town of Visby on which island?
questions.explanation: Gotland was a rich trading centre in the Baltic. The attack caused trouble with the Hanseatic League.

questions.question: Who became the first president of Iceland in 1944?
questions.explanation: He had led Iceland as regent since 1941, during World War II.

questions.question: Who is traditionally said to have founded Stockholm around the year 1252?
questions.explanation: Birger Jarl was a powerful Swedish leader, and his son became king.

questions.question: In 1448 the Danes chose Christian I as king. Which royal family did he start?
questions.explanation: Oldenburg kings ruled Denmark until 1863, when the Glücksburg branch took over.

questions.question: In which year did the Faroe Islands get home rule inside the Danish kingdom?
questions.explanation: Greenland got home rule 31 years later, in 1979.

questions.question: In 1874 which king became the first Danish king to visit Iceland, bringing it a constitution?
questions.explanation: The visit came during the celebration of 1,000 years since the settling of Iceland.

questions.question: Who was crowned in Kalmar in 1397 as king of Denmark, Norway and Sweden?
questions.explanation: Margrete I chose him as her heir, but she kept the real power until she died in 1412.

questions.question: Which governor freed the enslaved people in the Danish West Indies in 1848?
questions.explanation: He announced it on 3 July 1848, after thousands of enslaved people had risen up on St Croix.

questions.question: After Charles XII died in 1718, Sweden entered a period of parliamentary rule. What is it called?
questions.explanation: Parliament held the power until Gustav III took it back in 1772.

questions.question: Sweden's old parliament had four estates: nobles, clergy, townspeople and which group?
questions.explanation: Sweden kept this system until 1866, when a two-chamber parliament replaced it.

questions.question: The 1918 Act of Union between Iceland and Denmark could be ended after how many years?
questions.explanation: Iceland used that right and declared a republic in 1944.

questions.question: What was Nuuk, the capital of Greenland, called in Danish until 1979?
questions.explanation: Godthåb means Good Hope. Hans Egede founded the town in 1728.

questions.question: In 1850 Denmark sold its forts on the Gold Coast in West Africa to which country?
questions.explanation: The main fort was Christiansborg at Accra, later the capital of Ghana.
